opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about a lot, and honestly our approach is a little different from what a lot of robotics companies do. Historically, the way you'd build a robotics company is you'd pick one application, say, warehouse picking or a specific manufacturing step, and then you'd engineer the whole stack around that one task. That can work, but you end up building something very narrow, and a lot of the effort doesn't transfer to the next problem.

What we're really focused on is the foundation model itself: a general-purpose model that can control many different robots and do many different tasks. So when we think about applications, we're less asking "what's the one killer app we should go all-in on," and more asking "where can a general model already provide real value, and where will deploying it teach us the most?"

A few things guide that. One is the gap between what the model can do reliably today and what a task actually requires. Some tasks need extremely high reliability, and others are more forgiving: a human can step in occasionally, or a failure isn't catastrophic. Those forgiving settings are good places to start, because you can deploy before everything is perfect and still be useful.

Another is data. Deployment isn't just about revenue for us, it's a source of experience. If a robot is out in the world doing a task, it's collecting data on the long tail of situations you'd never think to stage in a lab, and that feeds back into making the model better across the board. So we like applications where there's a natural flywheel.

And the last thing is we try not to over-index on our own guesses. A lot of the most interesting use cases come from people who have a specific problem in their business that we'd never have thought of. So part of the strategy is making the models capable and adaptable enough that partners can fine-tune them for their setting with a relatively small amount of data, and then seeing where the pull actually is.

So it's a bit of a balance: keep pushing generality, because that's the long-term bet, while finding places where it's already good enough to be useful and where being out there makes the model better.

r001.rationale: The response says some tasks allow a human to step in occasionally, but it does not contrast human evaluation in successful machine-learning applications with the lack of routine human validation of robot action commands.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting in forgiving settings where occasional intervention is possible or failure is not catastrophic, which communicates seeking deployments that can tolerate mistakes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and honestly our approach is a little bit different from how I think a lot of robotics companies have historically operated. The traditional playbook is you pick a vertical early, you pick a task, and you build a company around solving that one task really well. And that makes a lot of sense if you believe the technology is going to be narrow.

But our thesis at Physical Intelligence is really that generality is the thing. We want to build a single model that can control lots of different robots and do lots of different tasks, and the whole premise is that the capabilities come from breadth of data and breadth of experience rather than from over-engineering a solution to one problem. So if we committed too early to a narrow application, we'd actually be working against our own thesis. We'd be optimizing for one thing when the point is to get the generalist model good.

That said, you can't just build a research lab in a vacuum forever. So the way I think about early applications is less "what's the first product" and more "where do we get signal." Where are the environments where the model is close enough to being useful that deploying it teaches us something real? Because the gap between a demo in the lab and a robot that actually works in someone's home or warehouse or kitchen is enormous, and you only learn what that gap looks like by going out and trying.

So we've done things like take the model to real homes it's never seen before and have it do laundry or clean up a kitchen, and the failures you see there are so informative. Lighting is different, the objects are different, someone put the trash can in a weird place. None of that shows up when you're iterating in a controlled setup.

In terms of what makes a good early application, I'd say a few things. One is tolerance for imperfection. If the task has to work 99.99% of the time on day one, that's probably not where you start. Two is whether the task sits in the sort of middle of the distribution of what the model has seen, so you're stretching it a bit but not completely. And three, honestly, is whether the deployment generates data and feedback that improves the model for everything else, not just for that one customer.

So I think of early applications as kind of a flywheel input rather than the destination. The destination is still the general model.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts narrow, task-specific robotics strategies with Physical Intelligence’s generalist-model approach, but it does not discuss human validation of outputs versus unvalidated robot action commands.

r002.rationale: It names “tolerance for imperfection” as a criterion for early applications and says tasks requiring 99.99% success on day one are not a good starting point.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to find places where the robot can do something useful relatively early, but where solving the problem also pushes us toward a more general capability. If you pick a task that’s completely repetitive and the environment never changes, there may already be a good automation solution. The interesting opportunities are tasks where there’s variation—in the objects, in how they’re arranged, in what someone is asking the robot to do—and that variation has made traditional automation difficult.

There’s also a practical question: How often does the robot need help, and what happens when it makes a mistake? A task can look really impressive in a demo and still not be useful if someone has to intervene every few minutes. So I’d look for applications where we can measure the value of the work, understand the reliability requirements, and have a reasonable way to recover when things go wrong.

And ideally, deployment creates a learning loop. The robot encounters new situations, we learn from those situations, and the model gets better. That makes an early application valuable both because it helps someone today and because it gives us a path toward doing a broader set of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intervention frequency and recovery from robot mistakes, but does not contrast human evaluation of outputs in machine-learning applications with the lack of routine human validation of robot commands.

r002.rationale: It recommends applications with a reasonable way to recover when things go wrong, communicating that deployment should be able to handle robot mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to find applications where the robot can do something useful today, but where solving that problem also pushes us toward more general capabilities. You can pick a very constrained task and engineer a system around it, but that doesn’t necessarily give you a path to a robot that can do lots of different things.

So I’d look for settings where there’s a family of tasks—different objects, different layouts, some variation in what people want the robot to do. You want enough structure that you can deploy and measure whether you’re actually helping, but enough diversity that the model has to learn something broadly useful.

And reliability matters a lot. A demo where something works most of the time is very different from a system that someone can depend on. So part of finding those early applications is understanding what happens when the robot makes a mistake. Can it recognize that, recover, or ask for help? The application and the model capabilities really have to develop together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and handling mistakes, but does not contrast human evaluation of machine-learning outputs with the lack of routine human validation of robot commands.

r002.rationale: It recommends applications with useful structure and discusses recognizing, recovering from, or asking for help after mistakes, but does not clearly propose deployment scenarios chosen because they can tolerate mistakes.
